358.title: Wrestling till daybreak (Genesis 32:22–32)
358.hook: Jacob wrestles all night, won't let go without a blessing, and limps away renamed
358.carry: I will not let thee go
358.howItsDone: The Catechism points to Jacob's night at the river as a symbol of prayer as a battle of faith and a triumph of perseverance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rachel and Leah: seven years like a few days, and the sister nobody chose. Your line was leah was seen. Who got your first attention? A new week, and a long night. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

In a side chapel of the church of Saint-Sulpice in Paris, there's a huge painting by Eugène Delacroix. A tree twisting up into the sky. In front of it, two figures locked together. One is a man, muscles straining, head down, pushing with everything he has. The other has wings, and stands almost calmly, one hand on the man's thigh. Twenty years have passed since Jacob ran from home. He's rich now, with wives, children, flocks. And tomorrow he has to face the brother who once planned to kill him, coming with four hundred men. Tonight, alone by a river, someone grabs him in the dark.
screen: `A PAINTING IN SAINT-SULPICE.` → `TWENTY YEARS, AND ESAU IS COMING.` → `ALONE BY A RIVER, IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: First, the fight. Jacob sends his family across the river Jaboc and stays behind alone. And a man wrestles with him until the breaking of the day. Who is he? Genesis just says a man. The prophet Hosea later calls him an angel. Jacob, by morning, says he has seen God face to face. The text leaves it open, and so does Delacroix. Second, the hold. The stranger can't overcome him, so he touches the hollow of Jacob's thigh, and it's put out of joint. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "Let me go, for it is break of day. He answered: I will not let thee go except thou bless me." Injured, exhausted, and still holding on. Third, the name. The stranger asks, what is thy name? And for the man who once said I am Esau to his father, the answer is a confession: Jacob. Heel-grabber. And the stranger says: "Thy name shall not be called Jacob, but Israel: for if thou hast been strong against God, how much more shalt thou prevail against men?" Israel, in Hebrew, sounds like one who strives with God, or God strives. A whole people will carry the name of a man who wrestled with God and wouldn't let go. Fourth, how the Church reads it. The Catechism calls this scene a symbol of prayer as a battle of faith and a triumph of perseverance. Jacob doesn't win by pinning anyone. He wins by holding on, and asking. And he walks away at sunrise blessed, renamed, and limping.
screen: `A MAN, AN ANGEL, OR GOD?` · `INJURED, AND STILL HOLDING ON.` · `HEEL-GRABBER BECOMES ISRAEL.` · `PRAYER AS A BATTLE OF FAITH.` · then, large: `I WILL NOT LET THEE GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold on in prayer a little longer, or, if you don't pray, stay with one hard question a little longer than usual. Settle, and breathe. Bring up something you've been wrestling with: a decision, a grief, a question about God, a fear about tomorrow. The usual move is to let go after a moment and reach for something easier. This time, don't. Stay with it through the whole bell. You don't need to win. Just keep hold. If you pray, you can use Jacob's words: I will not let thee go. The bell holds the time.
Israel. The new name Jacob is given after wrestling all night: one who strives with God. It becomes the name of a whole people.
Your line: I will not let thee go. Today, when you want to give up on something good because it's hard, hold on for one more round. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

359.title: Meeting Esau (Genesis 33)
359.hook: the brother he cheated runs and embraces him
359.howItsDone: Catholics pray "forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us" in every Our Father, and the Church teaches that being reconciled with others is bound up with being reconciled with God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Israel: a night of wrestling, a new name, and a limp. Your line was I will not let thee go. What did you hold on to? This morning, Jacob limps toward his brother. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

A name lights up on a phone: someone wronged years ago. A stomach can drop before a single word is read. Jacob has carried that dread for twenty years. When he fled, his brother was planning to kill him. Now he looks up, and there's Esau on the horizon, with four hundred men. Jacob has already sent wave after wave of gifts ahead: goats, sheep, camels, cattle, donkeys, hoping to soften him. He splits his family into groups. And then he limps out in front of all of them.
screen: `A NAME YOU DREAD ON YOUR PHONE.` → `ESAU, AND FOUR HUNDRED MEN.` → `JACOB LIMPS OUT IN FRONT.`

segments.voice: First, the bowing. Jacob bows to the ground seven times as he comes near his brother. The one who stole the blessing that said nations would bow to him now bows, again and again, to the brother he cheated. Second, the run. And here is the verse, in the Douay-Rheims: "Then Esau ran to meet his brother, and embraced him: and clasping him fast about the neck, and kissing him, wept." Esau runs. The wronged one moves first. No speech, no list of grievances, no condition. Third, the gifts. Jacob insists Esau keep the animals he sent ahead. Esau says, I have plenty, my brother; keep what is yours. And Jacob says something startling: seeing your face is like seeing the face of God. The night before, he wrestled God and called the place Phanuel, the face of God. Now he sees that face again, in the brother he feared. Fourth, the honesty. Genesis doesn't make it a fairy tale. Esau invites Jacob to travel with him; Jacob politely finds reasons to go his own way. The trust is new and fragile. But the brothers are at peace, and years later they stand together to bury their father. Some readers hear an echo in Luke's Gospel, in the parable of the prodigal son: the father sees his son a long way off, runs, falls on his neck and kisses him. In both stories the one with every right to stay away is the one who runs.
screen: `SEVEN BOWS TO THE GROUND.` · `ESAU RUNS FIRST.` · `YOUR FACE, LIKE THE FACE OF GOD.` · `A PEACE THAT'S NEW AND FRAGILE.` · then, large: `HE RAN TO MEET HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make the first move toward peace. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you're at odds with: a sibling, an old friend, a neighbor, a coworker. It doesn't matter who started it. Picture them on the horizon. Notice your stomach, your shoulders. Now picture the smallest possible step toward them. A short message. A like on their photo. Saying hello at the next family gathering. You don't need to fix everything. Just move first. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to run. The bell holds the time.
Meeting Esau. Twenty years after the stolen blessing, the brother who was cheated runs to Jacob, embraces him and weeps.
Your line: he ran to meet him. Today, take the small step you pictured toward someone you're at odds with, before you've worked out what you'll say. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

360.title: The coat and the dreams (Genesis 37:1–11)
360.hook: a favorite son, a colored coat, and brothers who can't speak peaceably
360.howItsDone: The Church reads the Joseph story in the weekday Mass during Lent, setting the brothers' envy beside the plot against Jesus in the Gospel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, meeting Esau: the wronged brother ran first. Your line was he ran to meet him. Did you take your small step toward someone? Today, the next generation, and the trouble starts again. Day three hundred sixty.

Some family photo albums have one: the kid in the middle of every picture. The one whose drawings went on the fridge, whose birthday got the bigger cake, who got away with things. A sibling can still name that kid, years later. Genesis has watched this pattern before. Isaac loved Esau more. Rebecca loved Jacob more. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah. And now Jacob, old, called Israel, has twelve sons, and he doesn't even try to hide which one is his favorite.
screen: `THE KID IN EVERY PICTURE.` → `A FAMILY OF FAVORITES.` → `TWELVE SONS, ONE FAVORITE.`

segments.voice: First, the favorite. Joseph is seventeen, the son of Rachel, the wife Jacob loved, born when Jacob was old. He tends the flocks with his older half-brothers and brings his father a bad report about them. Second, the coat. In the Douay-Rheims: "Now Israel loved Joseph above all his sons, because he had him in his old age: and he made him a coat of divers colours. And his brethren seeing that he was loved by his father, more than all his sons, hated him, and could not speak peaceably to him." Could not speak peaceably. Not even hello. Here's something honest about that coat: nobody is sure exactly what it looked like. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, gives it many colors. Some readers take the Hebrew phrase, ketonet passim, as a long robe, the kind the second book of Samuel says a king's daughters wore. Either way, it wasn't work clothes. It said: this one doesn't do what you do. Third, the dreams. Joseph dreams that his brothers' sheaves of grain bow down to his sheaf. Then that the sun, the moon and eleven stars bow down to him. And he tells them. Both times. The brothers hate him more. Even his father rebukes him: are your mother and I and your brothers to bow down to you? Fourth, the quiet line. The brothers envied him, Genesis says, but his father kept the matter in mind. Catholics may hear an echo in Luke, where Mary keeps things and ponders them in her heart. A father who caused the trouble also senses something in it he can't yet see.
screen: `SEVENTEEN, AND THE FAVORITE.` · `A COAT THAT SAID: NOT LIKE YOU.` · `SHEAVES AND STARS BOW DOWN.` · `HIS FATHER KEPT THE MATTER.` · then, large: `COULD NOT SPEAK PEACEABLY TO HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice favoritism around you. Settle, and breathe. Think through the places you spend time: your family, your workplace, your parish, your group of friends. Where is someone treated as the favorite, and someone else as the afterthought? Don't rush to blame anyone. Just see it. Then look honestly at yourself: is there anyone you favor without meaning to, a child, a coworker, a friend? And anyone you overlook? If you pray, you can ask for a fairer heart. The bell holds the time.
The coat and the dreams. Jacob's special robe for his favorite son, and Joseph's dreams of his family bowing down: the start of the long Joseph story.
screen: `THE COAT AND THE DREAMS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the coat caused trouble. Today, give one person you usually overlook the kind of attention you usually save for your favorite. Day three hundred sixty.

361.title: Into the pit (Genesis 37:12–36)
361.hook: the brothers sell Joseph for twenty pieces of silver
361.howItsDone: The Church keeps February 8, the feast of Saint Josephine Bakhita, a Sudanese woman sold into slavery as a child who became a Canossian sister, as a world day of prayer against human trafficking.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the coat and the dreams: a favorite son and brothers who couldn't say hello. Your line was the coat caused trouble. Who did you give your attention to? Today, the trouble comes due. Day three hundred sixty-one.

Jacob sends Joseph on an errand: go and see if your brothers are well, out with the flocks, and bring me word. It's a long walk from home. Joseph gets lost in the fields, and a stranger has to point him the right way. There he is on the last ridge, the boy in the coat, visible from a long way off. His brothers see him coming before he can see their faces. And one of them says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the dreamer cometh." By the time he reaches them, they've already decided what to do.
screen: `GO AND SEE IF YOUR BROTHERS ARE WELL.` → `THE COAT, SEEN FROM FAR OFF.` → `BEHOLD THE DREAMER COMETH.`

segments.voice: First, the plot. Come, the brothers say, let's kill him, throw him into a pit, say a wild beast ate him, and we'll see what becomes of his dreams. Reuben, the eldest, pushes back: don't kill him, just throw him in the pit. Genesis tells us why: he planned to come back later and rescue him. Second, the pit. They strip off the coat, that coat, and throw him into an old cistern. It's empty, the text says. No water in it. And then, without a word of comment from Genesis, they sit down to eat bread. Third, the sale. A caravan comes by, carrying spices down to Egypt. Judah speaks up: what profit is there in killing our brother? Let's sell him; after all, he's our brother, our own flesh. And they pull him out of the pit and, in the Douay-Rheims, "sold him to the Ismaelites, for twenty pieces of silver." Then Reuben comes back to the pit, finds it empty, and tears his clothes. Fourth, the lie. The brothers kill a young goat, dip the coat in its blood, and send it to their father. Do you know this coat? Jacob, who once wore goatskins to deceive his own blind father, is now deceived by goat's blood on his son's coat. He tears his garments and refuses to be comforted. I will go down to my son mourning, he says. Church Fathers such as Ambrose read Joseph as a figure of Christ: the beloved son, sent by his father to his brothers, rejected by his own, and sold for silver. Sold by his own, and carried down into Egypt.
screen: `LET'S KILL HIM, AND SEE HIS DREAMS.` · `AN EMPTY PIT, NO WATER.` · `TWENTY PIECES OF SILVER.` · `GOAT'S BLOOD ON THE COAT.` · then, large: `SOLD BY HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for anyone trafficked or sold, or, if you don't pray, hold them in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Joseph's story is ancient, but it isn't over. Somewhere today, people are bought and sold, forced to work, kept from home, sometimes by people who should have protected them. You may never know their names. Picture one person far from home who can't leave. Stay with them through the bell. If you pray, you can ask for their freedom, and for someone to find them. The bell holds the time.
Into the pit. Joseph, stripped of his coat, thrown into an empty cistern by his brothers, and sold for twenty pieces of silver into Egypt.
Your line: sold by his own. Today, learn one thing about modern trafficking, or about a group working against it, so the story doesn't stay ancient. Day three hundred sixty-one.

362.title: Prison (Genesis 39–40)
362.hook: a false accusation, prison, and a forgotten favor
362.howItsDone: The Joseph story is read at Mass on a weekday in Lent, and Psalm 105 (104 in the Douay numbering), which remembers Joseph in fetters, is among the psalms of the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, into the pit: the brothers stripped Joseph's coat, dropped him in a dry cistern, and sold him to traders bound for Egypt. Your line was sold by his own. Who did you hold in prayer? Day three hundred sixty-two.

Egypt. Joseph is a slave now, still a young man, bought by an officer of Pharaoh named Potiphar. And something odd happens: everything he touches goes well. Before long he's running the whole house. Then his master's wife starts noticing him, day after day, and one day, when no one else is inside, she grabs him by his cloak. He runs, and leaves the cloak in her hand. That's twice now a piece of Joseph's clothing has been turned into a lie. His brothers dipped his coat in goat's blood. She holds up his cloak and says he attacked her. Potiphar believes her. Joseph goes to prison. Today: the prison, and the sentence the text keeps repeating there.
screen: `A SLAVE IN POTIPHAR'S HOUSE.` → `A CLOAK LEFT IN HER HAND.` → `PRISON.`

segments.voice: Read chapter thirty-nine slowly and one phrase keeps coming back: the Lord was with Joseph. It's there when he's a slave in Potiphar's house. It's there when his master sees everything prospering in his hands. And it's there twice in the prison. "But the Lord was with Joseph," the Douay-Rheims reads, and soon the keeper of the prison puts him in charge of all the other prisoners. Notice where the sentence shows up. Not on the day he's made governor. In the slave quarters and in the cell. The text never says God got him out. It says God was with him in it. Second, what Joseph does when no one is looking. He refused his master's wife, and he gave two reasons: it would betray the man who trusted him with everything, and it would be a sin against God. Nobody was watching. That was the whole test. Third, the forgotten favor. Two of Pharaoh's officials land in the same prison: the chief butler, who poured Pharaoh's wine, and the chief baker. Each has a dream. Joseph sees their faces are sad one morning and asks why. He says interpretations belong to God, then tells them: in three days the butler goes back to his post, and the baker dies. Both come true. Joseph asks one thing of the butler: remember me to Pharaoh. And the chapter ends flatly. The butler forgot him. Two full years go by. Centuries later, a psalm looks back on this stretch of his life: his feet humbled in fetters, iron around him, until God's word came. Two years is a long time to be forgotten. The chapter doesn't hurry past it, and it never calls the waiting wasted.
screen: `THE LORD WAS WITH JOSEPH, IN THE CELL.` · `HE SAID NO WHEN NO ONE WAS WATCHING.` · `REMEMBER ME. THE BUTLER FORGOT.` · `A PSALM REMEMBERS THE FETTERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one right thing no one will see. Settle, and breathe. Walk through the rest of your day and find the moments nobody's checking: the dishes in the sink, the receipt that's slightly wrong in your favor, what you say about someone who isn't in the room. Pick one. Picture yourself doing the right thing there, quietly, with no credit and no audience. If you pray, you can carry the phrase from the chapter: the Lord was with Joseph. If you don't, just hold the choice for a minute and let it settle. The bell holds the time.
Prison. In Genesis, the place Joseph lands on a false charge, and where the text says, twice, the Lord was with him. Today's word.
Your line: the lord was with joseph. Today, somewhere no one's watching, do the right thing anyway, and let it stay unseen. Day three hundred sixty-two.

363.title: Pharaoh's dreams (Genesis 41)
363.hook: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner becomes governor
363.howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Joseph as patron of the universal Church, of workers and of families, and the old phrase Ite ad Ioseph, go to Joseph, appears in devotions to him, especially in March, the month traditionally given to Saint Joseph.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prison: a false charge, a cell, and a butler who forgot. Your line was the lord was with joseph. Where did you do right when no one saw? Day three hundred sixty-three.

Two years later, Pharaoh has a nightmare. He's standing by the Nile, and seven cows come up out of the river, sleek and fat, and graze in the reeds. Then seven more come up behind them, thin, ugly, all bone. And the thin cows eat the fat ones, and look no better afterward. He wakes, falls back asleep, and dreams again: seven full ears of grain on one stalk, swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones. Every wise man in Egypt is summoned. Nobody can explain it. And then the butler, the one who forgot, suddenly remembers: there was a young Hebrew in prison who read dreams. Joseph is pulled out of the dungeon, shaved, given clean clothes, and stood in front of the king.
screen: `SEVEN FAT COWS, SEVEN THIN.` → `NOBODY CAN EXPLAIN IT.` → `THE BUTLER REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: Pharaoh says he hears Joseph can read dreams. Joseph's first words turn that around: it isn't in him, he says; God will give Pharaoh his answer. Then the meaning. Seven years of plenty are coming to Egypt, and after them seven years of famine so heavy the good years will be forgotten. The dream came twice, Joseph says, because the thing is settled. Then he does something nobody asked him to do. He doesn't stop at the warning. He gives a plan. Find a wise man. Set overseers over the land. Take a fifth of the harvest in each good year and store it in the cities, so that when the lean years come, the country doesn't die. Pharaoh looks around his court and says, in effect, where would we find another man with the spirit of God in him? He puts his ring on Joseph's hand, dresses him in fine linen, hangs a gold chain around his neck, and makes him governor of all Egypt. Joseph is thirty. He was seventeen when his brothers sold him. Then it plays out exactly. Seven fat years, grain piled up like the sand of the sea. Then the famine, in every land. The people cry to Pharaoh for bread, and he answers in three words: "Go to Joseph." Catholics have borrowed that line for a different Joseph. Saint Joseph, the husband of Mary, also listened to dreams and also took his family down to Egypt, and in 1870 Pope Pius the Ninth named him patron of the whole Church. In Latin, Ite ad Ioseph, go to Joseph, appears in devotions to Saint Joseph.
screen: `NOT IN ME: GOD WILL ANSWER.` · `SEVEN YEARS FULL, SEVEN YEARS LEAN.` · `STORE A FIFTH IN THE GOOD YEARS.` · `GO TO JOSEPH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put something by for a lean time. Settle, and breathe. Think about the season you're in. If it's a full one, what could you store from it? A little money. A meal in the freezer. A thank-you note you could reread on a hard day. A friendship you could tend now, before you need it. If it's a lean season already, think back to a full one and notice what it left you. Choose one small thing to put by today. If you pray, you can offer the full years and the lean ones to God. If you don't, just sit with the thought of both. The bell holds the time.
Pharaoh's dreams. Seven fat cows and seven thin ones: a warning of plenty, then famine, that Joseph reads and turns into a plan. Today's word.
Your line: plan for the lean years. Today, set one thing aside, money or food or kindness, for a day that will need it. Day three hundred sixty-three.

364.title: The brothers come for grain (Genesis 42–44)
364.hook: Joseph tests them, and Judah offers himself for Benjamin
364.howItsDone: Some Catholic preaching sees in Judah's offer to take Benjamin's place a picture of Christ, whom the Book of the Apocalypse calls the lion of the tribe of Juda.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharaoh's dreams: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner made governor. Your line was plan for the lean years. What did you set aside? Today closes a week that began with Jacob wrestling till daybreak. Day three hundred sixty-four.

The famine reaches Canaan. Old Jacob hears there's grain in Egypt and sends ten of his sons to buy some. Not the youngest, Benjamin. He's Rachel's last son, and Jacob won't risk him. The ten arrive and bow down, faces to the ground, before the governor of Egypt. They have no idea who he is. Years have passed. He has an Egyptian name, Egyptian clothes, an interpreter between them. But he knows them the moment they walk in. And he remembers the dreams: sheaves of grain bowing down to his. Here they are, bowing, asking for grain. What would you do with your brothers in that room?
screen: `TEN BROTHERS GO DOWN TO EGYPT.` → `THEY BOW, AND DON'T KNOW HIM.` → `HE KNOWS THEM AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Joseph doesn't reveal himself. He tests them. First, he calls them spies and holds them three days. Then he keeps one brother, Simeon, and sends the rest home: bring your youngest back, and I'll believe you. And in front of him, thinking he can't understand, they talk in their own language: we are guilty about our brother; we saw his distress when he begged us, and we wouldn't listen. Joseph turns aside and weeps. Second, the hard road home. Jacob refuses to send Benjamin. Only when the grain runs out does Judah speak up: put the boy in my hands, and if I don't bring him back, let me bear the blame forever. Third, the trap. In Egypt, a feast, then a silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack. The steward chases them down, finds it, and the governor's verdict is simple: the one with the cup becomes my slave; the rest of you can go home. Here's the door the brothers walked through once before. Years ago they let Rachel's son be carried off to Egypt and went home without him. They could do it again, and this time it would even be legal. Fourth, Judah steps forward. He tells the whole story, the old father, the lost son, how the father's life is bound up in the boy's life, and then he asks: let me stay as your slave instead of him; let the boy go home. This is the same Judah who, years ago, had the idea of selling Joseph for silver. And Matthew's Gospel traces Jesus's family through Judah, the brother who offered himself. Look back over the week: a wrestler renamed Israel, Esau running to meet him, the coat, the pit, the prison, the dreams. A family that kept breaking, and now someone stands in the gap.
screen: `SPIES! THEY CONFESS THEIR OLD GUILT.` · `JUDAH PLEDGES HIMSELF FOR THE BOY.` · `A SILVER CUP IN BENJAMIN'S SACK.` · `TAKE ME INSTEAD OF HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one person you could stand in for. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone carrying something heavy right now: a coworker buried in a deadline, a parent with a sick kid, a friend stuck with a hard phone call. Ask what it would look like to take their place for an hour. Cover the shift. Make the call with them. Sit in the waiting room. Don't plan anything grand. Just one offer. If you pray, you can hold that person before God, the way Judah held his brother before the governor. If you don't, just keep them in mind for a minute. The bell holds the time.
The brothers come for grain. Hungry, guilty and bowing, they're tested, until Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place. Today's word.
screen: `THE BROTHERS COME FOR GRAIN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: judah stepped forward. Today, make one real offer to take something heavy off someone else's shoulders. Day three hundred sixty-four.

fork.setup: you're one of the brothers. the governor found his cup in Benjamin's sack. he says the boy stays as a slave and the rest of you can go home in peace. what do you do?
options: go home. it's legal, and it's not your fault.
fight your way out.
offer yourself as a slave in the boy's place.
fork.reveal: Judah steps forward, tells the whole story of the old father and the lost son, and asks to stay instead of Benjamin. the brothers who once sold Rachel's son won't leave this one.

original.note: Hebrew: grain for sale, the word Jacob uses when he hears there's grain in Egypt (Genesis 42:1–2).

trapdoor: what you thought: Joseph playing games with his brothers.
what it means: a test that puts them back where they once failed, with Rachel's son in danger, and this time Judah stands in his place.
what a scholar hears: Judah's plea fills Genesis 44:18–34, and the next chapter opens with Joseph unable to hold back.
